messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika, a 45-year-old Māori chef, came to treatment after nearly two years of living with the aftermath of a rape that had happened when he was leaving a late service alone. He described the assault plainly and with an unsettling ease, almost as if he could narrate it from outside himself, but when he tried to place the event in order his account collapsed into fragments. He could say where he had been, who was in the kitchen earlier that night, how he had walked to his car, and the fact that the attack happened in a dim stretch behind the building, yet he could not hold the memory together from one moment to the next. He would start to tell it, then cut himself off before the full image came into focus, pushing it away before he could feel everything at once. What made the memory so difficult to settle into a single sequence was that Mika had already come to believe the event had not only violated him but ruined the very parts of himself that used to organize his life.

Before the assault, Mika had defined himself by competence, speed, and control in the kitchen. He had built his identity around being the man who could run a service, calm a tense line, and stay composed when everyone else was under pressure. Afterward, he found himself thinking that he was no longer capable of the things that had made him who he was. He described standing at the pass and feeling, with a kind of shameful certainty, that the version of himself who could command a brigade and take pride in his work had been stripped away. He also felt dirty in a way he could not shake off, as though the assault had marked him permanently. Those beliefs were not abstract to him; they followed him into every part of the day and gave the event a meaning that was larger than the attack itself. Because he was convinced that his life had been destroyed by what happened, his own memories of the night kept breaking apart under the weight of what he believed they meant. He found himself unable to bear the story straight through, as if recalling it in full would confirm the finality of what he feared it had done to him.

In the months that followed, Mika kept going to work at first, but the restaurant became a place where the assault seemed to hover at the edge of everything. The back entrance where deliveries came in, the narrow corridor near the store room, and the sound of footsteps behind him after service all felt charged with the same threat. He began arriving early and leaving only when someone else was still nearby, and he avoided being the last one out, even if it meant staying after hours pretending to clean. He told himself it was safer not to think about what happened, because every attempt to look directly at it brought him back to the same conviction that he was no longer the man he had been. In practice, that meant he would talk about the assault very easily if asked, almost clinically, but only in a way that kept the memory at a distance; if he started to move toward the part that felt most painful, he would stop himself and shift to the next topic. The more he dwelled on being contaminated and broken, the more disordered the memory felt to him, and the less able he was to hold the event in a coherent order.

Mika’s relationships narrowed as a result. His divorce had already left him living alone, and after the rape he became increasingly certain that intimacy would only expose the contamination he felt in himself. He stopped going out with friends from work, turned down invitations to family gatherings, and let calls go unanswered when he knew people might ask how he was doing. At the restaurant, he remained reliable on the surface, but colleagues noticed he was quieter, more guarded, and increasingly unwilling to take on the kinds of responsibilities he once handled with ease. He hated that change most of all, because it seemed to confirm his own fear that the trauma had taken away what defined him. Even now, he could speak about the assault in a detached, matter-of-fact way, yet the story never stayed complete for long; it would fracture, blur, or be pushed back down before the worst parts could be fully remembered.

What finally brought Mika to seek help was a recent night shift when a junior cook accidentally came up behind him in the darkened hallway and he froze so completely that he had to grip the wall to stay upright. Afterward, he sat in his car for nearly an hour, staring at the steering wheel and thinking that his life had been destroyed and that he could not keep living as though the damage were temporary. He did not come in hoping to be told it was not that bad. He came because he was afraid that if he kept carrying the belief that he was ruined and contaminated, the memories would remain forever broken apart and his world would keep shrinking around them. More than anything, Mika said, he wanted to know whether anything of the man he had been could still be recovered.
